editorial_contributions.text: The following simple method will find small prime factors \(p\) of a number \(n\) in \(O(p^{1/2})\) arithmetical operations as opposed to the \(O(p)\) operations required by trial division. Let \(x_0=2\), \(x_{i+1}\equiv x_i^2-1\pmod n\) (other similar sequences may be used). Generate in turn the pairs \((x_j,x_{2j})\), accumulating the product \(\pmod n\) of the numbers \(x_{2j}.x_j\). At intervals, compute the g.c.d. of this product and \(n\), which may give a factor, not necessarily prime. Probabilistic arguments predict that on average one should take about \(1.03\,p^{1/2}\) steps to find a prime \(p\); this is confirmed by experiment. The method has been further discussed by \textit{R. K. Guy} [Proc. 5th Manitoba Conf. Numer. Math., Winnipeg 1975, 49--89 (1976; Zbl 0338.10001)].

title.title: A Monte Carlo method for factorization

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We describe some novel methods to compute the index of any integer relative to a given primitive root of a prime \(p\). Our first method avoids the use of stored tables and apparently requires \(O(p^{1/2})\) operations. Our second algorithm, which may be regarded as a method of catching kangaroos, is applicable when the index is known to lie in a certain interval; it requires \(O(w^{1/2})\) operations for an interval of width \(w\), but does not have complete certainty of success. It has several possible areas of application, including the factorization of integers.

title.title: Monte Carlo methods for index computation (mod \(p\))

editorial_contributions.text: Pollard's Monte Carlo (or ``rho'') method finds a factor \(p\) of \(N\) in \(O(\sqrt p)\) steps by consideration of \((x_{i+1} - x_i, N)\) for the sequence defined by \(x_{i+1}\equiv f(x_i) \pmod N\). The authors give evidence that, if the factors of \(N\) are known to be \(1 \pmod m\), then one should take \(f(x) =x^m +c\). Trial of this on Fermat numbers led, inter alia, to the factorization of \(F_8\) as \(1 238 926 361 552 897\) times a 62-digit number subsequently proved to be prime.

title.title: Factorization of the eighth Fermat number

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Since 1974, several algorithms have been developed that attempt to factor a large number \(N\) by doing extensive computations modulo \(N\) and occasionally taking GCDs with \(N\). These began with Pollard's \(p-1\) and Monte Carlo methods. More recently, Williams published a \(p+1\) method, and Lenstra discovered an elliptic curve method (ECM). We present ways to speed all of these. One improvement uses two tables during the second phases of \(p\pm 1\) and ECM, looking for a match. Polynomial preconditioning lets us search a fixed table of size \(n\) with \(n/2+o(n)\) multiplications. A parametrization of elliptic curves lets Step 1 of ECM compute the \(x\)-coordinate of \(nP\) from that of \(P\) in about \(9.3\, \log_2n\) multiplications for arbitrary \(P\).

title.title: Speeding the Pollard and elliptic curve methods of factorization
